title: Mouse papers reporting one enhancer deletion found a defect in 73% of deletions, papers reporting several in 41% (53% without 3 redundancy studies); conservation showed no detectable link
abstract: Deleting one enhancer from the mouse genome caused a reported defect in 58% of 226 published cases: in 73% when the paper reported only that deletion and in 41% when it reported two or more (53% without three studies of redundant enhancers); among these deletions, the evolutionary conservation of the deleted DNA showed no detectable link to a defect. This matters because papers that report one deletion probably give a too-high success rate for planning deletion experiments, and because conservation, the main evidence used to say which non-coding DNA has a function, did not separate deletions with and without a defect among the conserved candidates that investigators choose. An enhancer is a non-coding DNA region that increases transcription of a target gene. We took all 359 enhancers with a mutant allele in Mouse Genome Informatics (MGI, November 2026). Agent curators, blind to conservation, read the 293 linked papers and recorded whether mice that lose the enhancer had an organismal defect (death, malformation, or changed tissues, cell numbers, physiology, behaviour or fertility) beyond a change in target-gene expression. Their calls agreed with MGI's own curation in 91% of 74 shared cases (kappa 0.49), and an independent audit of 16 calls found no error. After removal of compound records that contain other deleted enhancers, 132 of 226 deletions (159 papers) had a defect (95% CI 49-68%, bootstrap over papers). The gap between single- and multi-deletion papers (odds ratio 3.8, 1.8-7.8) was smaller but held without the three redundancy studies (73% vs 53%; odds ratio 2.3, 1.2-4.4), after adjustment for loss of target expression, and without long or super-enhancer records; its cause (selective publication, choice of strong candidates, or study design) cannot be separated. Deleted enhancers were far more conserved than random annotated mouse enhancers; among them, the odds ratio for a defect was 1.06 per SD of phastCons coverage (0.74-1.51), so effects up to about 1.7 per SD are not excluded. Target-gene dosage sensitivity and nearby-enhancer number showed no clear link. Loss of target expression did go with a defect (71% vs 12% when expression was unchanged), and 32 of 94 deletions without a defect gave one in combination with other deletions. Limits: published deletions only, mostly targeted phenotyping, agent curation, narrow conservation range. We release the curated table with evidence quotes, 84 unphenotyped deletion lines, and testable predictions.

(a) Outcomes of single-enhancer loss alleles after adjudication (compound records and multi-enhancer blocks excluded). (b) Deleted enhancer features of 100-5,000 bp (orange) are far more conserved than length-matched random annotated mouse enhancers (blue): cumulative distribution of the mean phyloP in the best 50-bp window.

Univariable odds ratios (95% CI; standard errors clustered by paper) for an organismal defect after loss of one enhancer. Only the paper type (single- vs multi-enhancer paper) is clearly associated; conservation, target-gene dosage sensitivity and regulatory context show no detectable link. Loss of target expression (not shown; odds ratio 17 against unchanged expression) is the strongest correlate.
